title: ZINCOVIT vs ZINCOMED: Apex Labs Secures Madras HC Interim Injunction
summary: New Delhi: The Madras High Court has granted an interim injunction in favour of Apex Laboratories in a dispute over the sale of products under the name "ZINCOMED", which the company alleged infringed...

contentHtml:
New Delhi: The Madras High Court has granted an interim injunction in favour of Apex Laboratories in a dispute over the sale of products under the name "ZINCOMED", which the company alleged infringed its registered "ZINCOVIT" trademark and copyrighted packaging artwork.

Finding a prima facie case, the court observed that the respondents had copied a similar carton style and font, creating a likelihood of confusion among the public. It also recognised Apex’s prior use of ZINCOVIT and the goodwill and reputation built around the product over decades.

Justice P.B. Balaji passed the common order on November 13, 2026, in Original Application Nos. 1249, 1250 and 1251 of 2026, arising from C.S. (Commercial Division) No. 309 of 2026. The proceedings name Med Manor Organics and DM Pharma Private Limited as respondents. The order grants temporary protection while the underlying suit remains pending; it is not a final judgment deciding the infringement claims.

The suit concerns allegations of trademark infringement, copyright infringement and passing off. Apex’s case was that the respondents were selling products under ZINCOMED using a name and packaging presentation that imitated its established ZINCOVIT brand.

Through three applications, Apex sought separate but related temporary injunctions. The first concerned infringement of its registered ZINCOVIT trademark, Registration No. 487453 in Class 5, through the use of a deceptively similar mark.

The second sought protection against the alleged reproduction of its registered copyrighted artwork, Registration No. A 115854/2017. Apex alleged substantial copying of the colour scheme, get-up and layout of its labels or artistic works for the respondents’ ZINCOMED tablets, syrup, drops and other products.

The third application addressed passing off. Apex sought to restrain the respondents from presenting, or enabling others to present, ZINCOMED products as its own through manufacturing, selling, offering for sale, distributing, displaying, printing, stocking, using or advertising products bearing the disputed trademark or packaging artwork. The requested restraints extended to the respondents and persons acting through them, including their partners, agents, distributors, stockists and representatives.

Presenting the company’s background, advocate R. Sathish Kumar, appearing for Apex, submitted that the pharmaceutical company was incorporated in 1978, registered the ZINCOVIT trademark in 1988, and began using it in 1990. He placed the relevant suit documents before the court in support of the company’s claim to longstanding rights.

Counsel also submitted that sales turnover for ZINCOVIT alone exceeded Rs 320 crore in the last financial year. The order records this figure as part of Apex’s submissions without identifying that financial year by its specific dates.

Apex alleged that the respondents were imitating its trademark and selling their products under the name ZINCOMED. Its counsel drew the court’s attention to a comparison of the parties’ marks and packaging, arguing that the similarities were likely to confuse members of the public.

The company further relied on the status of the respondents’ trademark application. According to the submissions recorded in the order, the respondents had applied to register ZINCOMED on a “proposed to be used” basis. Apex relied on this circumstance alongside its earlier registration and use of ZINCOVIT to support its claim as the prior user.

On the timing of the proceedings, Apex submitted that it became aware of the alleged infringement only in August 2026 and thereafter promptly filed the commercial suit together with applications seeking urgent interim protection.

The order does not record any submissions or defence from the respondents. It records the hearing of Apex’s counsel and directs that notices be issued to the respondents. Their explanation for adopting ZINCOMED, their response to the alleged packaging similarities, and any challenge to Apex’s rights are therefore not available in this document.

Examining the material presented, Justice Balaji found visible similarities that justified interim intervention. The court observed:

"Prima facie, I am able to see that a similar style of carton has been copied and the font style has also been copied by the respondents/defendants."

The court also noted the likelihood of confusion among the general public. Taking account of Apex’s earlier registration and the respondents’ proposed-use application, it accepted Apex’s position as the prior user of ZINCOVIT and held that the company had established a prima facie case.

Its assessment also addressed the commercial interests at stake. The court noted that the dispute involved more than monetary loss, extending to the goodwill and reputation Apex had built over decades. These observations formed part of its consideration of the need for temporary protection.

The court separately considered whether Apex should first undergo pre-institution mediation under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. Relying on the company’s account that it discovered the alleged infringement in August 2026 and promptly sought relief, the court found sufficient grounds to dispense with that requirement because urgent interim relief was warranted.

The exact concluding portion of paragraph 6, granting that relief, reads:

"In view of the above, I am prima facie satisfied that the applicant has made out a case for the grant of urgent interim reliefs and dispensing with mandatory pre-institution mediation, as contemplated under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. In view of the above, there shall be an order of interim injunction as prayed for in these original applications.”

By granting the injunctions as sought in the three applications, the court extended interim protection against the alleged trademark infringement, reproduction of copyrighted packaging artwork and passing off described in Apex’s prayers.

The court also imposed a procedural compliance requirement on Apex. Paragraph 7 states:

"The applicant/plaintiff is directed to comply with the provisions under Order XXXIX Rule 3(a) of C.P.C and file necessary affidavit in the Court regarding compliance.”

Notices were directed to be served through the court and privately. The exact directions in paragraphs 8 and 9 read:

"Issue notice to the respondents through Court as well as privately, returnable by 08.01.2027.”

“Post the matter on 08.01.2027.”

The outcome is an interim injunction, with the respondents given notice and the matter scheduled for January 8, 2027.
